qs.q: What is the earliest detectable clinical sign of diabetic nephropathy that precedes a significant decline in the glomerular filtration rate?
qs.e: Microalbuminuria is the earliest detectable clinical sign of diabetic nephropathy, occurring subsequent to glomerular basement membrane thickening. Nodular glomerulosclerosis and CKD develop in later stages of the disease.

qs.q: A 32-year-old female presents with dysuria and frequency. Urine analysis confirms uncomplicated cystitis. Which medication should be avoided if she has a pre-existing reduced glomerular filtration rate?
qs.e: Nitrofurantoin is a first-line treatment for uncomplicated cystitis but must be avoided in patients with renal impairment due to reduced efficacy and increased toxicity. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and fosfomycin are alternative first-line agents.

qs.q: A laboratory test is ordered to evaluate a patient's estimated glomerular filtration rate using the MDRD formula. Which set of demographic and laboratory parameters are required for this calculation?
qs.e: The MDRD eGFR equation requires serum creatinine, patient age, gender, and race. Weight and height are not components of this specific estimating formula.

qs.q: Why is estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) frequently utilized alongside serum creatinine in renal assessment?
o: It completely eliminates the need to collect blood samples from patients with suspected kidney disease
It measures tubular reabsorption capacity directly without requiring any biochemical assays
It provides an estimate of filtration based on validated equations rather than relying on an isolated creatinine value
It serves as a specific diagnostic marker for myocardial injury and cardiovascular risk
qs.e: Estimated glomerular filtration rate provides an estimate of filtration based on validated equations. Creatinine alone is widely used, but eGFR aids renal assessment.
qs.s: Clinical Biochemistry and Laboratory Testing: Foundations and Workflow: MCQs

qs.q: In a patient evaluated for kidney function, which test is considered the best measure of the Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) and is linear with renal mass loss?
qs.e: Creatinine clearance is the best measure of GFR and is linear with renal mass loss, though it requires a 24-hour urine collection. Serum creatinine is affected by muscle mass and dietary meat intake, making it less precise on its own.
qs.s: Kidney Function Tests & Gastric Function: MCQs

qs.q: A patient with advanced renal parenchymal disease develops uremic acidosis. At approximately what threshold of the Glomerular Filtration Rate does this metabolic acidosis typically begin to manifest?
qs.e: Uremic acidosis develops when the GFR falls below 20 mL/min (corresponding to a creatinine greater than 350 micromol/L) due to combined glomerular and tubular failure leading to decreased hydrogen ion excretion.
qs.s: Kidney Function Tests & Gastric Function: MCQs

qs.q: Which term describes a patient with a glomerular filtration rate of 45 mL/min/1.73 m2?
qs.e: Chronic renal insufficiency refers to patients with mild-to-moderate renal impairment whose GFR falls between 30 and 90 cc/min. End-stage renal disease and chronic renal failure are reserved for significantly lower GFR thresholds.

qs.q: At approximately what glomerular filtration rate threshold does hyperkalemia typically develop due to decreased renal potassium excretion?
qs.e: Hyperkalemia usually develops when the GFR falls to less than 20-25 cc/min because of the decreased ability of the kidneys to excrete potassium. It can appear sooner in the presence of factors like NSAID use or a potassium-rich diet.

ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: GFR measures how much plasma the kidneys filter each minute. It reflects overall kidney health and guides diagnosis, staging, and treatment of renal disease.

sections.p: GFR is the volume of plasma cleared of waste per minute by the glomeruli. Normal adult GFR is ~90–120 mL/min/1.73 m²; it declines with age.
b: Low GFR → accumulation of urea, creatinine, fluid overload
High GFR may be seen in early diabetes or pregnancy

sections.p: Blood enters the glomerular capillaries under high pressure; filtration occurs across the fenestrated endothelium, basement membrane, and podocyte slit diaphragm into Bowman's space.
b: Filtration fraction ≈ 20 % of renal plasma flow
Starling forces (hydrostatic vs oncotic) drive filtration

sections.p: Autoregulation keeps GFR stable despite blood pressure changes via afferent arteriolar tone (myogenic response) and tubuloglomerular feedback (macula densa).
b: Angiotensin II constricts efferent arteriole → raises glomerular pressure
Prostaglandins dilate afferent arteriole → protect GFR

sections.p: Reduced GFR signals kidney injury. Causes are grouped by location: pre‑renal (hypoperfusion), intrinsic (glomerular, tubular, interstitial), post‑renal (obstruction).
b: Pre‑renal: dehydration, sepsis, heart failure, hepatorenal syndrome
Intrinsic glomerular: diabetic nephropathy, lupus, post‑infectious GN, HIV‑associated nephropathy, schistosomiasis
Intrinsic tubular: acute tubular necrosis from toxins, severe malaria, contrast, rhabdomyolysis
Post‑renal: obstructive stones, prostate hypertrophy, congenital anomalies

sections.p: GFR guides staging of chronic kidney disease (CKD) and dosing of renally cleared drugs. Sudden falls define AKI (KDIGO criteria).
b: CKD stages 1–5 based on eGFR thresholds
AKI: increase in serum creatinine ≥0.3 mg/dL in 48 h or ≥1.5× baseline in 7 d

t.b: What is the current filtration capacity? Elevated creatinine suggests reduced GFR; use equations (eGFR) for estimation.
When is creatinine unreliable? Provides GFR estimate independent of muscle mass; useful in malnutrition or extremes of age.
Is there acute renal failure? <0.5 mL/kg/h for >6 h signals AKI; monitor closely when labs unavailable.
